title: Monitor and Direct Personnel Performance and Conduct

lessons.title: Setting expectations and directing work
lessons.html:
Setting expectations and directing work

A feed mill shift supervisor or manager achieves results through people. Directing performance means making sure every team member knows what to do, has the means to do it, and gets feedback on how they are doing.

Clear roles and standards

  • Each position has a job description and the SOPs that apply to it: intake operator, mixer operator, pellet operator, bagging team, forklift driver.
  • Translate the production plan into shift tasks: who runs which line, which products, which cleaning and maintenance tasks.
  • Set measurable standards: tonnes per shift, batches without deviation, PDI results, housekeeping score, zero unsafe acts.

The shift briefing

  1. Safety first: any incidents, hazards or permits in force today.
  2. Production plan and priorities, including changeovers and medicated runs.
  3. Quality issues from the previous shift.
  4. Allocation of people and tasks.
  5. Questions and concerns from the team.

Keep it short, standing, and at the same time every shift. Record attendance and key points.

Competence and allocation

Allocate people only to tasks they are trained and authorised for, especially forklifts, boiler operation, confined space work and hot work. Keep a skills matrix that shows who is competent on what, and use it to plan cover for leave and to identify training needs. Pair new operators with experienced ones.

Monitoring on the floor

  • Walk the floor regularly. Observe work against the SOP, not just results.
  • Check records during the shift: batch sheets, checklists, lockout registers.
  • Give immediate, specific feedback: recognise good work and correct deviations straight away and respectfully.
  • Stop unsafe work at once. Any team member also has the right and duty to stop unsafe work.

lessons.title: Managing performance and conduct fairly
lessons.html:
Managing performance and conduct fairly

South African labour law requires employers to treat employees fairly. The Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 and its Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, and the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997, set the framework. Your company's disciplinary code and procedures apply these; always follow them and involve HR.

Performance versus conduct

IssueExampleApproach
Poor performance (capacity)Operator repeatedly makes batching errors despite tryingFind the cause, train, coach, set a review period, give support
MisconductBypassing an interlock, absence without permission, coming to work under the influenceFollow the disciplinary code: investigate, hearing, fair sanction

Managing poor performance

  1. Meet privately. Describe the standard and the gap with facts and records.
  2. Listen to the employee's explanation. Look for causes: training, equipment, unclear instructions, personal or health issues.
  3. Agree an improvement plan: actions, support, timeframe and review date.
  4. Follow up and document each review.
  5. If performance still does not improve after fair support, escalate according to policy.

Handling misconduct

  • Act promptly and consistently: the same rule applied to everyone.
  • Gather facts: statements, records, CCTV where available.
  • Ensure the employee knows the allegation, has time to prepare, can be represented as the code allows, and can state their case.
  • Sanctions are progressive for less serious matters: verbal warning, written warning, final written warning. Serious misconduct may justify dismissal after a fair process.
  • Keep written records of every step.

Motivation and recognition

Most people want to do good work. Recognise good results at briefings, involve operators in solving problems, explain the reasons behind rules, and develop people through training and acting opportunities.

Key points

  • Set clear standards and brief the shift daily, safety first.
  • Allocate only trained, authorised people to tasks; keep a skills matrix.
  • Monitor work on the floor and give immediate, specific feedback.
  • Separate poor performance from misconduct and handle each fairly.
  • Follow the company code, the LRA framework and involve HR.
